transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-02
Start: 16:00 PDT
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Alex Morgan (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Jason Lee (CTO - Atlas HealthTech), Maya Patel (Infra), Samir Rao (Head of ML)

Summary (auto-gen, rough): POC scoping call to decide between Redwood hosted, dedicated, or private deployment for Atlas HealthTech pilot. Discussed workload sizing, success criteria (latency, throughput, quality), benchmarks, timeline (2-6 week POC), security/compliance constraints (HIPAA, KMS, VPC), and next steps.

Topics:
- Success criteria and acceptance tests
- Workload characteristics and sizing
- Benchmark plan and metrics (p50/p90/p99 latency, tokens/sec, cost per 1M tokens, quality/regression)
- Deployment tradeoffs: Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private (latency, cost, isolation, operational burden)
- Timeline and ownership

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex: hey everyone thanks for joining, uh we'll kick off, i'm alex from redwood, with priya, our se, quick roll call?
[00:08] Jason: jason here, hi everyone, thanks for setting this up
[00:11] Maya: maya here, infra lead at atlas
[00:14] Samir: samir here, ml lead
[00:16] Priya: priya from redwood, hi!
[00:18] Alex: cool, agenda is quick intro, then dig into your workload sizing and success criteria, talk through hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs, and then the benchmark plan and timeline. sound good?
[00:27] Jason: yep, lets go

[02:05] Samir: to give context, our goal is to power clinical note summarization and some chat workflows for internal clinicians. rough qps is around 40 concurrent users at peak, burst up to maybe 200 during rounds, typical message length is 200-400 tokens, sometimes up to 1k for longer notes.
[02:28] Maya: infra note: data is PHI, so we need HIPAA controls, audit logs, preferably customer-managed keys and VPC peering or private link. we can't have patient data leaving our region without controls.
[02:40] Alex: totally, that's helpful. in terms of success criteria, what are your acceptance thresholds? latency, quality, and cost tradeoffs?
[02:49] Jason: from product side, p99 interactive latency ideally < 300ms, p90 < 150ms. throughput needs to handle those bursts, and cost is secondary but we want to keep unit cost reasonable. quality — summaries must be within 5% of current human baseline on Rouge/clinical metrics; we can be more specific.
[03:12] Priya: ok noted. typical POC acceptance we see: latency SLOs at p90/p99, throughput targets (tokens/sec or requests/sec), and quality regression bounds compared to your eval set. we'll include automated evals in the benchmark.

[05:01] Alex: now on deployment modes at a high level — hosted is fastest to iterate and you get our managed runtime, auto-scaling, and lower ops. Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools for predictable throughput and lower unit costs at scale plus isolation. Private (VPC/on-prem) gives you full network control and customer-managed keys and is used for strict compliance but slower to stand up.
[05:26] Samir: question, does hosted support customer-managed KMS and VPC?
[05:30] Priya: hosted supports VPC peering/private-links in many cases, and we can integrate with customer KMS in dedicated/private modes; for hosted, key management is more limited — we can do envelope encryption and we have SOC2 controls but if you need keys in your HSM we usually recommend private or dedicated with KMS options. sometimes we can do bring-your-own-key for higher tiers, but it's dependent on the contract.

[07:12] Maya: for us, we need full KMS control and audit logs with 7-year retention. that pushes us away from simple hosted unless you have those certs.
[07:25] Alex: understood. for the POC we can run hosted as a trial if you anonymize data, or go dedicated with stricter controls. private will take longer to stand up (on-prem or VPC private control plane) — usually 4-8 weeks for initial infra depending on change windows.

[09:40] Samir: about benchmarks: we'd like to run our model + prompt on the same sequences and measure p50/p90/p99 token latency, throughput (tokens/sec), and cost per 1M tokens. we also want quality checks — rouge scores and clinical error rates. do you have a benchmark harness?
[09:58] Priya: yes we have a benchmark template and scripts, we can run with your dataset. typical test matrix includes varying sequence lengths (128, 256, 512, 1k), batch sizes (1, 4, 8), generation parameters, and warm vs cold cache behavior. we also measure KV/prefix caching impacts for chat use cases.

[12:03] Jason: what's the difference in observed latency between hosted and dedicated GPUs? do you have numbers?
[12:10] Priya: roughly, hosted with shared pools for small models can give similar latencies to dedicated at low QPS, but under sustained load dedicated shows better p99 and consistent throughput because of reserved GPU capacity and tuned kernels. dedicated also allows pinned model versions and kernel/quantization profiles which can reduce cost further. hosted is faster to start but may have more noisy neighbors unless you choose a higher tier.

[14:20] Maya: any model constraints — we plan to use an open encoder-decoder model tuned for medical summarization; will Redwood handle quantized variants and kernel selection?
[14:28] Priya: yes we support quantized variants (8-bit, 4-bit profiles) and the runtime picks kernels based on architecture, sequence length patterns, and hardware. we'll recommend configs in the optimize report. there can be small quality regressions with aggressive quantization — we'll include regression thresholds in the tests.

[16:55] Alex: on cost modeling, we usually show delta between hosted per-token pricing vs dedicated reserved capacity. for your QPS, we can run a quick cost estimate once we have expected token volumes. dedicated typically pays off when you have stable sustained load and can commit to a monthly reserved capacity.

[18:44] Samir: timeline for POC: what's realistic for us to get results?
[18:48] Alex: typical POC timeline for this type is 3-6 weeks: week 0 to set success criteria and data handoff, week 1 run initial hosted experiments (or dedicated small pool warmup), week 2 run full benchmark matrix including dedicated variants, week 3 analyze results and run evals, then a decision/cutover plan. if you go private/on-prem it pushes to 6-8+ weeks total for setup.

[21:02] Jason: we might want an initial hosted proof that uses anonymized data to validate quality quickly, while parallelly prepping for dedicated with KMS for final acceptance.
[21:12] Alex: that's a common path — fast hosted proof then dedicated pilot. we just need your thumbs on what counts as success.

[23:30] Maya: security questions — do you provide SAML SSO for console access, RBAC, and audit logs? also network egress limits, and whether we can lock down endpoints to our VPC?
[23:40] Priya: yes SAML/SSO supported, RBAC integrated with SSO groups, audit logs can be streamed to your SIEM, and we support private endpoints/vpc peering. for egress we can provide Egress NAT or private link; specifics depend on dedicated/private vs hosted. we'll share the security checklist.

[25:55] Samir: benchmark specifics: for the baseline we want p99 < 300ms for 200-token responses at peak QPS, throughput >= 120 reqs/sec sustained, and cost per 1M tokens under $X (we'll define X after you send sample calc). quality: no more than 2% drop in clinical extraction metrics vs our offline pipeline.

[27:10] Priya: i'll capture that; we'll include noise controls and run both warm and cold cache measurements. also we'll surface KV cache hit rates — for many chat flows prefix caching reduces latency significantly.

[29:01] Alex: on the engineering side, what infra access will we need to run dedicated or private benchmarks?
[29:08] Maya: for dedicated: network peering, an IAM role for read-only access to an S3 bucket with sample dataset, and a small jump host for troubleshooting. for private: obviously more engagement with security and on-prem teams.

[31:12] Jason: are there any gotchas around HIPAA and data residency for hosted?
[31:18] Priya: hosted can be HIPAA-supporting in many regions with SOC2 controls, but for strict KMS/HSM requirements and long-term logs we usually recommend dedicated or private. we also provide BAAs for qualifying customers — we'll pull legal into that thread.

[33:40] Samir: on evaluation, can you produce a reproducible report with all scripts and metrics so we can hand that to our compliance team?
[33:48] Priya: yes the benchmark harness produces an artifact bundle: raw logs, per-request latencies, token counts, converted cost estimations, and evaluation metrics. we'll share a link to the benchmark spreadsheet and the run artifacts.

[35:55] Maya: what's the rollback plan if the POC fails to meet thresholds after dedicated commit?
[36:01] Alex: typical options: extend tuning and quantization profiles, test different model variants, or fallback to hosted for a temporary period. we'll document the canary/rollout and A/B approach in the runbook.

[38:30] Samir: are there any customer references or case studies in healthcare for dedicated/private?
[38:36] Alex: yes we have a couple anonymized case studies; i'll share redacted references. one had similar constraints and moved from hosted pilot to dedicated reserved capacity after 2 months.

[40:05] Priya: operational items for the benchmark: we recommend test windows to avoid interfering with production, and to include spike tests to simulate rounds (200 QPS) and sustained runs to measure thermal performance. also collect memory/GPU utilization for kernel tuning.

[42:18] Maya: can we run the benchmark against your hosted environment first to get a quick read?
[42:22] Alex: yes, if you can anonymize or synthetic-ize the data. or we can run with toy data but the quality numbers won't be meaningful. recommended: you provide a de-identified dataset and we'll run hosted tests within 3-5 business days after data handoff.

[44:55] Jason: pricing — what will you need to estimate cost? tokens/day, expected retention, peak terabytes egress?
[45:02] Alex: tokens/day, avg tokens per request, concurrency profile, expected model size and whether you need embedding storage or long-term logs — that lets us run a per-token hosted estimate and a reserved capacity recommendation for dedicated. we'll include amortized infra costs and expected break-even point.

[47:30] Samir: about model versions: can we pin a version and control rollouts so we can test quality regression over time?
[47:35] Priya: yes version pinning, canary rollouts, and auto-fallback are supported. we can tie evals to rollouts so if quality drops we trigger rollback.

[49:50] Maya: timeline recap and owners?
[49:55] Alex: recap — Alex sends pricing, benchmark spreadsheet, SOC2 and security checklist by 4/6. Maya provides de-identified dataset and network details by 4/9. Samir defines exact quality metrics (clinical metrics and thresholds) by 4/8. Priya prepares benchmark plan and schedule for week of 4/13. follow-up meeting to review results 4/20.

[51:10] Jason: sounds good, let's do hosted quick check then plane for dedicated benchmark.

[53:02] Alex: thanks everyone, we'll send notes and the attachments. Priya will set up the benchmark run and we'll loop in legal for BAA and SOC2. talk soon.

Notes: shared artifacts referenced during call: benchmark_template.xlsx (link: tinyurl.com/atlas-redwood-benchmark), security_checklist.pdf (link placeholder), SOC2_report_link (link placeholder).

End of transcript.
